extracted.intended_audience: readers seeking advice on conversation, disputation, and social conduct (educated/general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for how to converse, dispute, and profit from conference: who to converse with, what conduct to avoid, how to value form and truth, and how to use examples (good and bad) for self-improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer conversation over mere book-study
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of books is a languishing and feeble motion that heats not, whereas conversation teaches and exercises at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversation combines teaching and exercise; the author would sooner consent to lose sight than hearing and speech. Use active verbal exchange to train the mind rather than relying solely on reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose interlocutors who challenge you
rubrics_metrics.description: If I converse with a strong mind and a rough disputant, he presses upon my flanks, and pricks me right and left; his imaginations stir up mine; jealousy, glory, and contention, stimulate and raise me up to something above myself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek out vigorous, disputatious companions who will rouse and improve your thinking rather than flatter or placate you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constant company of weak or mean spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis not to be expressed how much [the mind] loses and degenerates by the continual commerce and familiarity we have with mean and weak spirits; there is no contagion that spreads like that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent interaction with weak minds degenerates one's own faculties; be selective about habitual company to preserve intellectual vigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make disputation a spectacle for the great
rubrics_metrics.description: To do it as a spectacle and entertainment to great persons, and to make of a man’s wit and words competitive parade is, in my opinion, very unbecoming a man of honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid performative disputation intended to amuse or impress superiors; argument should be for truth and improvement, not display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to and tolerate diverse and odd opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: No propositions astonish me, no belief offends me, though never so contrary to my own; there is no so frivolous and extravagant fancy that does not seem to me suitable to the production of human wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give hearsay and vulgar opinions at least a hearing; refusing to do so risks obstinacy. Even silly or popular beliefs deserve consideration to avoid fanaticism or closed-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Welcoming contradiction as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: When any one contradicts me, he raises my attention, not my anger: I advance towards him who controverts, who instructs me; the cause of truth ought to be the common cause both of the one and the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive contradiction cheerfully and use it to test and correct your own view; take pleasure in being reproved when it assists truth, provided reproach is not imperious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain order and method in argument
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not so much require force and subtlety as order; I mean the order which we every day observe in the wranglings of shepherds and shop-boys, but never amongst us... their tumult and impatience never put them out of their theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep to the subject, structure an argument coherently, and preserve the thread of dispute; chaos, digressions, and interruptions are fatal to productive discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passion and anger in disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: What will the angry man answer? Passion has already confounded his judgment; agitation has usurped the place of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow anger or agitation to replace reason; passion undermines judgment and the pursuit of truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict disputation with fools and the ill-bred
rubrics_metrics.description: Our disputes ought to be interdicted and punished as well as other verbal crimes... Plato in his Republic prohibits this exercise to fools and ill-bred people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or forbid argument with those incapable of rational discourse; debating such persons disperses the subject and annihilates truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and avoid abusive disputational tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: One flies to the east, the other to the west; they lose the principal... another deafens you with prefaces and senseless digressions... a last man sees nothing into the reason of the thing, but draws a line of circumvallation about you of dialectic clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of interlocutors who use digressions, railing, sophistry, extreme rhetoric, plausibly irrelevant dialectic, or appeals to bluster; these defeat the subject rather than illuminate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value manner/form as much as content
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis my humour as much to regard the form as the substance, and the advocate as much as the cause... to speak methodically, prudently, and fully, is a talent that few men have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate method, prudence, and completeness of expression; the way one argues (form) materially affects its force and reception, not only the raw truth of the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at truth, not mere victory or display
rubrics_metrics.description: To hunt after truth is properly our business, and we are inexcusable if we carry on the chase impertinently and ill; when you get the better of your argument, 'tis truth that wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct disputes as a search for truth; avoid treating argument as combat for reputation. Let truth be the shared goal between disputants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct, well-formed criticism to formalistic or petty attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: I receive and admit of all manner of attacks that are direct, how weak soever; but I am too impatient of those that are made out of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept straightforward critique even if it is blunt; react with impatience to attacks that are merely formal, ceremonious, or evasive in form rather than substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bad examples as useful negative models
rubrics_metrics.description: I make use of those that are ill, which are everywhere to be found: I endeavour to render myself as agreeable as I see others offensive...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by avoiding others' faults; negative examples (ridiculous, awkward behaviour) can instruct more effectively than positive exemplars in reforming oneself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be moderate in reproach; avoid tyrannic sourness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is equally vicious both in him that is in the right, and in him that is in the wrong; for 'tis always a tyrannic sourness not to endure a form contrary to one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether right or wrong, do not be tyrannically sour toward dissenting forms or opinions; cultivate patience and self-awareness rather than reproachful anger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge others only after self-judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever should find himself, his son, and a stranger guilty of any violence and wrong, ought to begin with himself... he should at least present himself the first to the punishment of his own conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by examining and judging yourself before reproving others; self-scrutiny gives moral authority and humility to criticism of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be seduced by externals—titles, robes, and pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: As in conference, the gravity, robe, and fortune of him who speaks, ofttimes gives reputation to vain arguments and idle words... the words, but the grimaces also of these people, are considered and put into the account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist being persuaded solely by a speaker's rank, dress, or bearing; require that claimed experience be shown to yield distilled understanding, not merely a list of offices or travels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience must be distilled into reasoned conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The fruit of a surgeon’s experience... is not the history of his practice... unless he knows how thence to extract something whereon to form his judgment... they must weigh, sort and distil them, to extract the reasons and conclusions they carry along with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept bare tallies of experience; insist that practitioners analyze, generalize, and present the reasoning that follows from their experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning is valuable but harmful if undigested
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning improves fortunes enough, but not minds; if it meet with those that are dull and heavy, it overcharges and suffocates them... 'tis a very useful accession to a well-born soul, but hurtful and pernicious to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure learning is assimilated and applied; mere accumulation of erudition without discernment can make a person worse rather than better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence can be a prudent posture for the great
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence is to them, not only a countenance of respect and gravity, but very often of good advantage too... Whilst they torment us with this complication and confusion of words, it fares with them, methinks, as with jugglers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those of high station may benefit from measured silence to avoid exposing ignorance or inviting scorn; speech should match one's competence.
